title: The same program, two ways of running it
caption: A container carries the software its program needs, so the computer underneath only needs Docker.
description: Two panels. On the left, a Python program written for Python 3.13 runs directly on a computer that has Python 3.9 installed, and it fails or behaves differently. On the right, the same program runs inside a container that also holds Python 3.13, and it runs the same wherever Docker runs.

title: From image to finished program
caption: A container runs only as long as its main process. When that process finishes, the container stops but is not deleted.
description: A sequence in four steps. An image made of Python and Alpine Linux layers sits on disk. docker run creates a container holding the image's files plus an empty writable layer, in the Created state. Docker starts python as the main process and the container is Running. Python prints Hello from inside a container and exits with code 0, so the container shows Exited (0) and docker logs still shows the message.

steps.label: Start with an image
steps.text: The image holds a set of files: Alpine Linux and Python. On its own it does nothing; it is a template.

steps.label: docker run creates a container
steps.text: Docker makes a container from the image: the image’s files, shared and read-only, plus a thin, empty writable layer of its own.

steps.label: The main process starts
steps.text: Docker starts the command you gave, python, inside the container. While it runs, the container is running.

steps.label: The program finishes
steps.text: Python prints its message and exits with code 0. With its main process gone, the container stops. Docker keeps the container, and its logs, until you remove it.

title: The docker command and the Docker Engine
caption: You type docker commands; the Docker Engine does the work of storing images and running containers.
description: A terminal on the left sends docker run and docker ps requests to the Docker Engine on the right. Inside the engine are stored images, such as python, postgres, and redis, which it uses to create containers, some running and one exited.

title: An image is a stack of layers
caption: docker history lists the newest layer first, which is the same order as the top of the stack.
description: On the left, simplified docker history output lists four rows from newest to oldest: a settings-only row of 0 bytes, a 44.1 MB layer that installs Python, a 2.94 MB layer that adds system packages, and a 9.31 MB layer that adds the Alpine Linux files. On the right, the same three file layers are drawn as a stack, with Python on top and Alpine Linux at the bottom, all read-only and shared by every container.

title: Where a container’s changes go
caption: Each container has its own writable layer. The image underneath never changes.
description: A sequence in five steps. One read-only image sits at the bottom. Containers A and B are created from it, each with its own empty writable layer. A process in container A writes /tmp/note.txt, which appears only in A's writable layer. A process in container B runs cat /tmp/note.txt and gets No such file or directory. Finally container A is removed along with its writable layer and the note, while the image and container B are unchanged.

steps.label: One image
steps.text: The image’s layers are read-only and stored once, however many containers use them.

steps.label: Two containers
steps.text: Each container made from the image gets its own empty writable layer on top.

steps.label: Container A writes a file
steps.text: A process in container A creates /tmp/note.txt. The new file goes into A’s writable layer; the image is unchanged.

steps.label: Container B looks for it
steps.text: Container B sees the image plus its own writable layer, which is still empty, so it has no note.

steps.label: Remove container A
steps.text: Removing container A deletes its writable layer and the note with it. The image and container B are untouched.

title: One main process, and extra ones from docker exec
caption: docker exec adds a process to a running container. The container’s life still depends only on process 1.
description: A terminal runs docker run with sleep infinity, which starts process 1, the main process, inside a container. A second command, docker exec with ps, adds an extra process to the same container. Both processes see the same files. Notes explain that the extra process can finish without stopping the container, but the container stops when process 1 finishes.

title: How a request reaches a server in a container
caption: Publishing connects a port on your computer to a port inside the container. Using 127.0.0.1 keeps it private to your computer.
description: A sequence in four steps. A web server inside a container listens on port 8000. A curl request from the terminal on your computer cannot reach it, because the container has its own network. After publishing with -p, the request goes to 127.0.0.1 on an assigned port such as 54321 and Docker forwards it to port 8000 in the container. Another device on your network is refused, because 127.0.0.1 means this computer only.

steps.label: A server inside the container
steps.text: The web server listens on port 8000 on the container’s own private network.

steps.label: No way in yet
steps.text: A request from your computer cannot reach port 8000. The container’s network is separate, and nothing connects the two.

steps.label: Publish the port
steps.text: -p connects your assigned port on 127.0.0.1 to port 8000 inside the container. Docker forwards each request across.

steps.label: Only this computer
steps.text: Because the port is published on 127.0.0.1, other devices on your network cannot connect. Without that address, they could.

title: A bind mount shares one folder with a container
caption: The container sees your folder directly. The ro option lets it read the files but not change them.
description: On the left, your computer has the folder DOCKYARD_WORKSPACE/site containing index.html. On the right, the container sees the same folder at /site containing the same index.html. A two-way arrow says they are the same files, not a copy. Editing the file on your computer is seen by the server at once, and a tag says ro: cannot write.

title: Every part of the web server command
caption: Everything before the image configures the container. Everything after it is the main process.
description: The docker run command for the web server, one option per line, with a note beside each: -d runs in the background; --name gives the name used in later commands; --label marks it as this lab's container; -p connects your port on this computer to port 8000; -v makes your folder appear at /site read-only; -w starts the process in /site; the image variable is the image to start from; and python -m http.server 8000 is the main process.

title: Intent survives a missing Pod
caption: A simplified model of a Deployment controller, separate from your real lab.
description: An interactive model with a desired replica count, a list of observed Pods that can be deleted, and a button that advances the controller one step toward the desired count.

title: The Pod and its data have different lifetimes
caption: A simplified model of Pods, claims, and volumes, separate from your real lab.
description: An interactive model in which you remove a Pod, its PersistentVolumeClaim, and its PersistentVolume, and change the reclaim policy to see which deletions destroy the stored records.

title: A majority and a route are separate requirements
caption: A simplified model of etcd quorum and a load-balanced API endpoint, separate from your real lab.
description: An interactive model with three control-plane nodes, each running an etcd member, and a load balancer that can route to any of them; you stop members, choose routes, and try a write to see whether it succeeds.

title: How one job travels through Dispatch
caption: The finished Dispatch: the API accepts work, the worker does it, PostgreSQL remembers it, and Redis passes the news between them.
description: A sequence in four steps showing you, the API, Redis, PostgreSQL, and the worker. You send a job titled hello to the API. The API saves it in PostgreSQL with the status queued, notifies Redis, and replies that it was accepted. The worker hears about the new job, takes it, converts hello to HELLO, and saves the result in PostgreSQL with the status done. Finally you ask the API, which reads PostgreSQL and replies with status done.

steps.label: Send a job
steps.text: You send a job to the API: a short piece of text, such as hello.

steps.label: The API records and announces it
steps.text: The API saves the job in PostgreSQL with the status queued, pushes a short notification onto the Redis queue, and replies to you straight away.

steps.label: The worker does the work
steps.text: The worker hears about the new job, takes it from the database, converts its text to uppercase, and saves the result with the status done.

steps.label: Ask for the result
steps.text: Later you ask the API about your jobs. It reads them from PostgreSQL and replies with each job’s status and result.

title: How Dispatch grows through the course
caption: Each stage adds the parts, and the skills, the next one depends on.
description: A timeline in four stages. In module 1, Dispatch is only its API, running in one container. In modules 2 to 6, all four parts, the API, Redis, the worker, and PostgreSQL, run together with Docker Compose. In modules 7 to 12, Kubernetes runs two copies each of the API and worker alongside Redis and PostgreSQL. In modules 13 to 24, three copies run on a cluster you build yourself, with monitoring and security added.

steps.label: Module 1: the API alone
steps.text: Dispatch starts as one web service in one container. It answers a health request so you can tell it is working.

steps.label: Modules 2–6: all four parts
steps.text: You build Dispatch’s own image, then run the API, Redis, the worker, and PostgreSQL together with Docker Compose, keeping the data safe.

steps.label: Modules 7–12: on Kubernetes
steps.text: Kubernetes keeps several copies of the API and worker running, routes requests to them, stores data on persistent volumes, and rolls out new versions safely.

steps.label: Modules 13–24: run like a real service
steps.text: You add capacity limits, monitoring, automated delivery, and security, then build and repair the Kubernetes cluster underneath it yourself.

title: Dispatch’s first version in this lab
caption: The same pattern as the foundations web server: a published port in, and a read-only folder of code mounted.
description: On your computer, a curl request to /healthz goes to 127.0.0.1 on an assigned port such as 54321, which is published with -p to port 8080 in the container. Inside the container, python app.py runs the Dispatch API on port 8080 and replies with status ok. The workspace folder containing app.py is bind mounted read-only at /app inside the container.

title: A container’s states and the commands that move it
caption: Stopping a container keeps it. Only docker rm removes it.
description: A state diagram. docker create makes a Created container from an image; docker start moves it to Running; docker stop, or the process ending, moves it to Exited; docker start runs an exited container again; and docker rm moves an exited container to Removed. A dashed shortcut shows docker run as create plus start. Notes say docker ps lists running containers and docker ps -a lists created and exited ones too.

title: Same name, same container?
caption: A name is just a label. The ID tells you whether it is really the same container.
description: A sequence in four steps. A container named dispatch has the ID 3f2a9c and its own logs and files. Stopping and starting it keeps the same ID. Removing it deletes its ID, logs, and files, and frees the name. Running a new container with the same name produces a different ID, 9d41e7, with no logs or files yet.

steps.label: A new container
steps.text: Docker gives the container a unique ID. The name is a friendlier label pointing at it.

steps.label: Stop and start
steps.text: Stopping and starting keeps the same container, so the ID, logs, and files are all unchanged.

steps.label: Remove it
steps.text: docker rm deletes the container, including its logs and writable layer. Its name is now free.

steps.label: Run again with the same name
steps.text: A new container can reuse the name, but it gets a new ID and starts with no logs or files. It only looks like the old one.

title: Where a container’s logs come from
caption: Docker records both output streams of the main process, so you can read them later.
description: Inside a container, the main process python app.py writes to standard output and standard error. Docker stores both streams as the container's logs. docker logs in your terminal reads them back, for example a line showing GET /healthz 200. A note says logs remain after the container stops, until it is removed.

title: What docker stop actually does
caption: SIGTERM asks the process to finish. SIGKILL ends it without asking.
description: A sequence in three steps. docker stop sends SIGTERM to process 1. A well-behaved process closes its connections and exits, leaving Exited (0). A process that ignores SIGTERM is sent SIGKILL after about ten seconds and is killed with no clean-up, leaving Exited (137).

steps.label: docker stop sends SIGTERM
steps.text: Docker asks the main process to finish by sending it the SIGTERM signal.

steps.label: A well-behaved process exits
steps.text: The process closes its connections and exits by itself. The container shows Exited (0).

steps.label: A process that ignores it
steps.text: If the process does not exit, Docker waits about ten seconds, then sends SIGKILL. The process ends immediately with no clean-up, and the container shows Exited (137).

title: What each Dockerfile instruction contributes
caption: Some instructions add layers of files; CMD only records a setting for later.
description: A sequence in four steps beside the worked example Dockerfile. ARG and FROM start from the supplied Python image, whose Python and Alpine Linux layers form the base. WORKDIR and COPY add a layer containing /tool/report.py. CMD records the setting start: python report.py, which adds no files. Finally, docker run starts containers from the finished image.

steps.label: FROM picks the starting image
steps.text: The build begins with every layer of the supplied Python image.

steps.label: WORKDIR and COPY add files
steps.text: WORKDIR sets the folder, and COPY adds report.py there as a new layer on top.

steps.label: CMD records the start command
steps.text: CMD adds no files. It records which command a container should run when it starts.

steps.label: Run containers from the image
steps.text: The build is finished. Every container made from this image starts with report.py and runs python report.py.

title: The build context
caption: Docker builds only from the files it was sent; .dockerignore keeps the rest on your computer.
description: Your folder, the build context, contains Dockerfile, app.py, VERSION, .dockerignore, secret.env, and a cache folder. The folder is sent to docker build, where COPY can use only what it was sent. A note says .dockerignore lists secret.env and cache, so they are never sent.

title: A change has to travel through three things
caption: Editing a file changes neither the image nor the container, and building a new image does not change a running container.
description: A sequence in four steps with three columns: your VERSION file, images, and containers. At first the file, the image tagged practice, and the running container all have dispatch-1. Editing the file to dispatch-2 changes only the file. docker build creates a new image with dispatch-2 and moves the practice tag to it, but the container still serves dispatch-1 from the old, now untagged image. Replacing the container creates a new one from the new image, which serves dispatch-2.

steps.label: Everything matches
steps.text: The file, the image tagged practice, and the running container all hold dispatch-1.

steps.label: Edit the file
steps.text: Saving VERSION changes only the file in your workspace. The image and container are unchanged.

steps.label: Build the image
steps.text: docker build makes a new image with dispatch-2 and moves the practice tag to it. The running container still uses the old image.

steps.label: Replace the container
steps.text: Removing the old container and running a new one from the tag finally serves dispatch-2.

title: Which build steps run again
caption: Put files that change rarely before files that change often, so slow steps stay cached.
description: A sequence in three steps beside a five-line Dockerfile: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY requirements.txt, RUN pip install, and COPY service. On the first build every step runs. After editing only the service source, the first four steps are reused from the cache and only COPY service runs again. After editing requirements.txt, FROM and WORKDIR are reused, but COPY requirements.txt and every later step run again.

steps.label: The first build
steps.text: With nothing cached yet, every step runs.

steps.label: Edit the source code
steps.text: Only the final COPY used a changed file, so the slow package installation is reused from the cache.

steps.label: Edit requirements.txt
steps.text: The second COPY now sees a changed file, so it and every later step run again, including the installation.

title: Two stages, one final image
caption: The verify stage can hold anything the build needs; the final stage receives only what you copy into it.
description: Two regions. Stage 1, verify, starts from the base image, holds app.py, VERSION, and generated __pycache__ files in /source, and runs py_compile on app.py. Stage 2, the final image, starts from the base image again, receives only app.py and VERSION in /app through COPY --from=verify, and sets USER 10001:10001. A note says only the final stage becomes the image you run.

title: A running container behind the wrong mapping
caption: The host side of a mapping can be right while the container side points where nothing listens.
description: A sequence in two steps. At first, a curl request to 127.0.0.1 port 49152 is forwarded to port 8081 in the container, but Dispatch listens on 8080, so nothing answers and the request fails. After the container is replaced with a mapping to 8080, the same request reaches Dispatch and returns status ok.

steps.label: Forwarded to 8081
steps.text: Docker forwards the request to port 8081, where nothing is listening. The container is running, but the request fails.

steps.label: Replaced with a mapping to 8080
steps.text: The replacement container forwards the same host port to 8080, where Dispatch listens, so the request succeeds.

title: 127.0.0.1 depends on where you stand
caption: Each container has its own network environment, so its localhost is itself.
description: Three side-by-side places: your computer, the API container, and another container. In each, a request to 127.0.0.1 arrives back in that same place: this computer, the API container, or that container. A note says 127.0.0.1 always means the place making the request, never a neighbor.

title: Connecting two containers by name
caption: A shared user-defined network gives containers a path and a name to use; no published port is needed between them.
description: A sequence in three steps. Your terminal requests /dependency from the API through its published port. With no shared network, the API cannot resolve the name dependency. After both containers join the lab network, with the alias dependency on the dependency container, the API's request to dependency:8080 succeeds because Docker's DNS turns the name into the current address. The dependency still has no published port.

steps.label: No shared network
steps.text: The API can be reached from your computer, but it has no network in common with the dependency, so the name dependency means nothing to it.

steps.label: Join one network
steps.text: Both containers are attached to the lab network, and the dependency’s connection carries the alias dependency.

steps.label: Call it by name
steps.text: The API asks for dependency:8080. Docker’s DNS answers with the dependency’s current address, and the request succeeds.

title: Why the API’s request never leaves its container
caption: Test from the caller’s own network environment, then fix the setting by replacing the caller.
description: A sequence in three steps on the lab network. The API's upstream setting is 127.0.0.1:8081, so its request loops back into the API container, where nothing listens, and is refused. A docker exec test from inside the API container shows that http://dependency:8080 works. The API container is replaced with the upstream setting dependency:8080, and its request now reaches the dependency.

steps.label: The configured address
steps.text: 127.0.0.1:8081 points back into the API’s own container. Nothing listens there, so the connection is refused.

steps.label: Test from inside the API
steps.text: docker exec runs a request from the API container’s own network environment. The dependency’s name and port work.

steps.label: Replace the API
steps.text: A replacement API container with the corrected setting reaches the dependency over the lab network.

title: Where /data can live
caption: A mount moves the data out of the container’s writable layer, so replacing the container leaves it behind.
description: Three columns, each with a container writing /data/jobs.db. With no mount, the data goes into the container's own writable layer and is lost with the container. With a bind mount, it goes into a folder you chose on your computer and survives replacement. With a named volume, it goes into a Docker-managed volume and survives replacement. A note says neither mount protects against deleting or corrupting the data itself.

title: Replacing the container, keeping the data
caption: The storage outlives the container because it was never inside it.
description: A sequence in three steps. A container with /data mounted writes a job into separate storage holding jobs.db. The container is removed, and the storage remains. A replacement container with the same mount at /data reads the job back, so GET /jobs still returns keep this job.

steps.label: Write a job
steps.text: The container writes the job into jobs.db on the mounted storage, not into its own writable layer.

steps.label: Remove the container
steps.text: Removing the container deletes the container, but the mounted storage is separate and remains.

steps.label: Mount it again
steps.text: A replacement container with the same mount sees the same jobs.db, so the job is still there.

title: A numeric owner mismatch
caption: Linux compares numbers: the process’s UID must be allowed by the directory’s owner and mode.
description: A sequence in three steps. The Dispatch API runs as UID 10001, but /data on the volume is owned by 0, root, with mode 0700, so writing fails with permission denied. A temporary container runs chown 10001:10001 /data, making UID 10001 the owner. The write then succeeds while the API still runs as an ordinary user. A note says chmod 777 or running as root would also work by giving far more access than the API needs.

steps.label: The write is denied
steps.text: The API runs as UID 10001, but the directory belongs to UID 0 with mode 0700, which admits only its owner.

steps.label: Change only the owner
steps.text: A temporary maintenance container changes the directory’s owner to 10001, then removes itself.

steps.label: The write succeeds
steps.text: The API, still running as UID 10001, now owns the directory and can save jobs.

title: Back up, restore, and prove it
caption: The source stays untouched; the API is stopped only while its own database is replaced.
description: A sequence in four steps. A temporary container reads the source volume's jobs.db read-only and writes backup.tar into your workspace with tar -c. The Dispatch API that uses the target volume is stopped. Another temporary container extracts the archive into the target volume and changes the owner. The API is started again and GET /jobs finds the recovered job.

steps.label: Archive the source
steps.text: A temporary container mounts the source read-only and writes backup.tar into your workspace.

steps.label: Stop the target’s API
steps.text: Stopping the API makes sure nothing writes to the target database while it is replaced.

steps.label: Restore into the target
steps.text: Another temporary container extracts jobs.db into the target volume and gives it to UID 10001.

steps.label: Start and verify
steps.text: With the API running again, request /jobs and look for the recovered job, then write a new one.

title: Recovery point and recovery time
caption: A recent backup shrinks the lost data; a practised restore shrinks the outage.
description: A timeline. A backup is taken, which is the recovery point; later a failure happens; later still service is restored. Changes made between the backup and the failure are lost. The time between the failure and the restored service is the recovery time.

title: Dispatch as one Compose project
caption: Compose starts all four roles on one network; only the API is published to your computer.
description: compose.yaml is read by docker compose up, which starts four services on the network app. The api service has a published port reached from 127.0.0.1 on your computer. The worker, queue (Redis), and db (PostgreSQL, with the jobs volume) have no published ports. The api and worker each connect to the queue and the db by their service names.

title: Interpolation versus a container’s environment
caption: ${…} is filled in from your terminal when Compose reads the file; only environment entries reach the container.
description: Three stacked panels. Your lab terminal has variables such as DOCKYARD_DB_PASSWORD, DOCKYARD_PORT, and HOME. In compose.yaml, the environment section sets DB_HOST to db and DB_PASSWORD to ${DOCKYARD_DB_PASSWORD}, which Compose fills in while reading the file. Inside the api container, only DB_HOST and DB_PASSWORD exist; HOME and DOCKYARD_PORT are not passed in.

title: Running is not the same as ready
caption: service_healthy makes the API wait for its dependencies’ health checks, not just for their containers to exist.
description: A sequence in three steps with three services: db with the pg_isready check, queue with redis-cli ping, and api with GET /readyz, which depends on the other two. At first db and queue are running but still starting, and the api waits. Then db and queue become healthy, and the api starts. Finally the api's own check passes, all three are healthy, and docker compose up --wait finishes successfully.

steps.label: Containers start
steps.text: db and queue are running, but their health checks do not pass yet. The api waits, because it depends on them being healthy.

steps.label: Dependencies become healthy
steps.text: pg_isready and redis-cli ping succeed, so Compose starts the api.

steps.label: The API is ready too
steps.text: The api’s own check of /readyz succeeds, so every service is healthy and docker compose up --wait finishes.

title: Two workers, one jobs table
caption: Replicas share the queue and database; row locks decide which worker takes each job.
description: Worker 1 and worker 2 both hear from the queue that work is available. In the jobs table in PostgreSQL, job 1 is locked by worker 1, job 2 is locked by worker 2, and job 3 is still queued. A note says each worker skips jobs another worker has locked, so a job is claimed once.

title: A logical backup restored beside the live database
caption: The application keeps using dispatch; restored exists only to prove the backup works.
description: One PostgreSQL server in the db container holds two databases. The api and workers use dispatch, the live database. pg_dump writes dispatch out to backup.sql in your workspace, and psql reads backup.sql into a separate database named restored, used only as a recovery test.

title: Reading an image reference
caption: A reference ends with either a tag, which can move, or a digest, which identifies fixed content.
description: Two image references with their parts labelled. In 127.0.0.1:49804/dispatch:release, 127.0.0.1:49804 is the registry, dispatch is the repository, and release is a tag that can move. In 127.0.0.1:49804/dispatch@sha256:3f1a…, the registry and repository are the same, and sha256:3f1a… is a digest identifying fixed content.

title: A tag moves; a digest stays
caption: Deploy by digest when you need to know exactly which image will run.
description: A sequence in two steps. In the registry, the tag dispatch:release and the digest reference dispatch@sha256:3f1a… both point at image A. Then someone pushes image B, sha256:9c2e…, under the same tag. The tag now points at image B, so a deploy by tag gets image B, while the digest reference still points at image A, so a deploy by digest still gets image A.

steps.label: After your push
steps.text: The tag release and the digest sha256:3f1a… both identify image A.

steps.label: Someone pushes again
steps.text: A new image B is pushed under the same tag. The tag moves to B; the digest still identifies A.

title: One image name, several platforms
caption: Docker picks the image that matches your processor from the name’s list.
description: The image name python points to a list of platform images. One is linux/arm64, for ARM64 processors, which an Apple Silicon Mac pulls. The other is linux/amd64, for x86-64 processors, which an x86-64 PC pulls.

title: Deleting a secret does not remove it
caption: Keep secrets out of the build context; a later layer can only hide what an earlier one stored.
description: A sequence in three steps showing image layers beside what the running container sees and what the image stores. COPY . . copies app.py and .env into a layer, so both the container and the image contain .env. Adding RUN rm .env hides .env from the running container, but the image still stores it in the COPY layer. With .env listed in .dockerignore, the COPY layer contains only app.py, and no layer stores .env.

steps.label: COPY . . copies the secret
steps.text: Everything in the folder, including .env, is stored in the COPY layer.

steps.label: Deleting it later only hides it
steps.text: RUN rm .env adds a layer that hides the file from the running container, but the COPY layer below still stores it.

steps.label: .dockerignore keeps it out
steps.text: With .env listed in .dockerignore, the build never receives it, so no layer can contain it.

title: Independent layers of restriction
caption: If one layer is bypassed, the others still apply.
description: Nested layers around Dispatch, which runs as UID 10001. From the inside out: all capabilities dropped, no new privileges, a read-only filesystem, and cgroup limits of 128 MiB memory, half a CPU, and 64 processes. A note says each layer closes a different door and together they limit the damage.

title: The objects behind one application
caption: You describe the Deployment; Kubernetes creates the ReplicaSet and Pods, and the Service sends requests to them.
description: A Deployment with replicas 2 manages a ReplicaSet that keeps 2 Pods running. The ReplicaSet creates two Pods, each holding a Dispatch container. A Service, which provides a stable address, sends requests to both Pods. A note says you change the Deployment and Kubernetes creates and replaces the rest.

title: From kubectl apply to running Pods
caption: apply records what you want; controllers and the node do the work afterwards.
description: A sequence in four steps. kubectl apply sends the manifest to the API server, which stores the desired state and replies that the deployment is configured, though nothing is running yet. The Deployment controller notices it wants 2 Pods but sees 0. It creates two Pods, which start on the node. Finally both Pods are 1/1 ready and kubectl rollout status reports a successful rollout.

steps.label: apply is accepted
steps.text: The API server stores your desired state and replies at once. No container has started yet.

steps.label: A controller notices
steps.text: The Deployment controller compares what you asked for with what exists: it wants 2 Pods and sees 0.

steps.label: Pods are created
steps.text: The controller creates Pods, and the node starts their containers. Until they pass their checks, they are only starting.

steps.label: The rollout finishes
steps.text: Both Pods are ready, so kubectl rollout status reports success. This is the moment the change has really happened.

title: How a Service chooses its Pods
caption: A selector matches labels exactly; one wrong character leaves the Service with nowhere to send requests.
description: A sequence in two steps. The Service dispatch has the selector app=dispatch. Two Pods labelled app=dispatch are selected and a Pod labelled app=worker is not, so the EndpointSlice lists 2 ready Pod addresses. When the selector is mistyped as app=dispach, no Pod matches, and the EndpointSlice is empty.

steps.label: The selector matches
steps.text: Both Pods labelled app=dispatch are selected, and their ready addresses appear in the EndpointSlice.

steps.label: One wrong character
steps.text: With the selector app=dispach, no Pod matches. The Service still exists, but its EndpointSlice is empty.

title: Namespaces inside one cluster
caption: Names only need to be unique within a namespace; some objects belong to the whole cluster.
description: A cluster containing three namespaces. The dispatch namespace holds the Service dispatch and your Pods. A staging namespace also holds a Service named dispatch, which is allowed because it is a different namespace. The kube-system namespace holds Kubernetes itself and should be left alone. Nodes and other cluster-wide objects belong to no namespace.

title: What a context combines
caption: Switching context changes which cluster, login, and namespace your next command uses.
description: Inside the kubeconfig file named by KUBECONFIG, a cluster entry says where the API is, a user entry says how to log in, and a namespace such as dispatch is the default. A context combines the cluster, the user, and the namespace. The current-context setting points at one context, and every kubectl command goes to it.

title: A careful change, step by step
caption: The first three steps cost nothing and catch most mistakes before they reach the cluster.
description: Five steps in a row: render fills in the image, diff shows what would change, a server dry run checks the object, apply saves it in the cluster, and rollout status confirms the Pods are ready. The first three change nothing; the last two change the cluster. A note says to check which context you are using before any of these steps.

title: Five controllers, five shapes of work
caption: Choose the controller by how the work should behave, not by habit.
description: Five panels. A Deployment runs interchangeable copies, as many as you ask for. A DaemonSet runs one Pod on each matching node, shown with node 1 and node 2. A StatefulSet runs db-0 and db-1, each with its own stable name and data volume. A Job runs a Pod that does its task until it succeeds and is Completed. A CronJob uses a schedule such as 0 2 * * * to create a new Job, which creates a Pod.

title: Why the DaemonSet wants zero Pods
caption: A DaemonSet’s desired count comes from the nodes it may use.
description: A sequence in two steps. The DaemonSet's node selector requires a label ending node=missing, which the lab's node does not have; its labels include kubernetes.io/os=linux. No label matches, so DESIRED is 0 and no Pod is placed. When the selector matches the node, DESIRED becomes 1 and a node-agent Pod runs on it.

steps.label: No node matches
steps.text: The node selector asks for a label no node has, so the DaemonSet wants zero Pods.

steps.label: The selector matches
steps.text: Once the selector allows the lab’s node, the DaemonSet wants one Pod there, and runs it.

title: What kubectl port-forward connects
caption: The tunnel goes straight to one Pod, and exists only while the command runs.
description: On your computer, curl sends a request to 127.0.0.1 port 18080, where kubectl port-forward is listening. kubectl uses the Service dispatch only to choose one of its Pods, then carries the request through a temporary tunnel straight to that Pod, where the API listens on port 8080. A note says requests do not pass through the Service.

title: Init containers, sidecars, and a shared folder
caption: Init containers finish first; main containers and sidecars share files only through the same volume.
description: A sequence in three steps inside one worker Pod with the containers configure, worker, and observer and an emptyDir volume named shared. First the init container configure runs and writes worker.conf into shared while the others wait. Then configure has completed, and worker and the observer sidecar both read worker.conf from shared. In the broken version, the observer mounts a different emptyDir named scratch, which is empty, so it cannot see the file.

steps.label: The init container runs first
steps.text: configure writes worker.conf into the shared emptyDir. The main containers wait until it finishes.

steps.label: Then the main containers
steps.text: worker and the observer sidecar start, and both read worker.conf from the same volume.

steps.label: A different volume shares nothing
steps.text: If the observer mounts another emptyDir, it sees that volume’s empty folder instead of the file.

title: Completions, parallelism, and a retry
caption: At most two Pods run at once, and the Job keeps going until five have succeeded.
description: A timeline with two slots for completions 5, parallelism 2, and backoffLimit 2. Slot 1 runs Pod 1, Pod 3, and Pod 5, all successful. Slot 2 runs Pod 2, which succeeds, then Pod 4, which fails, then a retry, which succeeds. The Job reaches 5 of 5 completions and is Complete. A note says a failed Pod counts toward backoffLimit and the Job retries with a new Pod.

title: A schedule meeting a slow run
caption: concurrencyPolicy decides what happens when a run is still going at the next scheduled time.
description: A timeline for the schedule */5 * * * * with concurrencyPolicy Forbid. At 02:00 a Job runs and succeeds. At 02:05 a Job starts and is still running at 02:10, so the 02:10 run is skipped. At 02:15 a new Job runs and succeeds. A note says kubectl create job --from=cronjob starts a run immediately without waiting.

title: Two ways a ConfigMap reaches a container
caption: The same ConfigMap can feed an environment variable and a mounted file, and they behave differently.
description: The ConfigMap dispatch-settings holds environment: learning and a banner.txt key. Inside the API container, the environment key becomes the environment variable DISPATCH_ENV, read once at start, and banner.txt becomes the mounted file /config/banner.txt, which is kept up to date. Dispatch's /config address shows both.

title: When a ConfigMap change arrives
caption: Mounted files follow the ConfigMap; environment variables wait for a new container.
description: A sequence in three steps. At first the ConfigMap has environment learning and banner v1, and the running Pod shows DISPATCH_ENV=learning and banner.txt v1. After the ConfigMap is edited to testing and v2, the mounted banner.txt updates to v2 within a minute or two, but DISPATCH_ENV still shows the old value learning because it is read only at start. After kubectl rollout restart, a new Pod shows DISPATCH_ENV=testing and banner v2.

steps.label: Pod and ConfigMap agree
steps.text: The running Pod read the environment name at start and sees the banner file v1.

steps.label: Edit the ConfigMap
steps.text: The mounted file updates in place within a minute or two. The environment variable keeps its old value.

steps.label: Restart the rollout
steps.text: New Pods read the environment variable again when they start, so both values now match the ConfigMap.

title: Base64 is not encryption
caption: A Secret is protected by who can read it, not by its encoding.
description: You write password: example. The Secret stores it base64-encoded as ZXhhbXBsZQ==. Anyone who can read the Secret can decode it back to example. Real protection comes from controlling who may read Secrets, encryption at rest, and applications that never print them.

title: A projected volume combines sources
caption: Several Secrets and ConfigMaps can appear as files in one folder.
description: The Secret dispatch-database with its password key and the ConfigMap dispatch-settings with two keys both feed one projected volume. Mounted at /etc/dispatch in the container, it contains the files password, environment, and banner.txt.

title: How the API answers a Pod’s request
caption: Authentication names the caller; authorization checks what its bound Roles allow, in that namespace.
description: A sequence in four steps. The inventory Pod sends a request with the token for the ServiceAccount dispatch-reader. The API server's authentication step identifies it as system:serviceaccount:dispatch:dispatch-reader. Its authorization step follows the RoleBinding in dispatch to a Role that allows only listing Pods. Listing Pods in dispatch returns 200 OK. Listing Secrets in dispatch returns 403 Forbidden. Listing Pods in kube-system returns 403 Forbidden, because the binding applies only in dispatch.

steps.label: Who is asking?
steps.text: The token identifies the caller as the ServiceAccount dispatch-reader in the dispatch namespace.

steps.label: List Pods in dispatch
steps.text: The RoleBinding in dispatch gives this ServiceAccount a Role that allows listing Pods, so the answer is 200.

steps.label: List Secrets
steps.text: The Role says nothing about Secrets, so the API refuses with 403. The request arrived; RBAC said no.

steps.label: List Pods in kube-system
steps.text: The RoleBinding only applies in dispatch, so the same request in another namespace is refused with 403.

title: Where each Service type lets clients in
caption: ClusterIP serves the inside of the cluster; NodePort and LoadBalancer add doors from outside.
description: A cluster containing the Service dispatch, which sends traffic to two Pods. Another Pod inside the cluster reaches the Service through its ClusterIP. Your computer reaches it through a node port such as node:30080, the NodePort path. An outside client reaches it through a load balancer address on port 8080, the LoadBalancer path. A note says each type builds on the one before it.

title: port versus targetPort
caption: port is what clients use; targetPort must be where the application actually listens.
description: A sequence in two steps. A client connects to the Service on port 8080. With targetPort 8080, the Service forwards to port 8080 in the Pod, where Dispatch listens, and the request succeeds. With targetPort 9090, the Service forwards to port 9090, where nothing listens: endpoints still exist, but every connection is refused.

steps.label: targetPort matches the listener
steps.text: The Service forwards from its port 8080 to the Pod’s port 8080, where Dispatch is listening.

steps.label: targetPort is wrong
steps.text: The Service still selects the Pods, so its endpoints look healthy, but it forwards to 9090, where nothing listens.

title: How an Ingress request is served
caption: The Ingress is only rules; the controller reads them, terminates HTTPS, and forwards to the Service.
description: Your client sends an HTTPS request for https://dispatch.test/ to Traefik, the ingress controller. Traefik reads the Ingress rules, which send dispatch.test/ to dispatch:8080, and takes its certificate from the Secret dispatch-tls holding tls.crt and tls.key. It forwards the request over HTTP to the Service dispatch on port 8080, and from there to the Pods.

title: The two checks HTTPS makes
caption: Trust and hostname are both checked before any data is exchanged.
description: A sequence in three steps. Traefik presents a certificate for dispatch.test from the practice certificate authority to curl. With --cacert, curl trusts the issuer and confirms the hostname, so the request continues. Without --cacert, the issuer is unknown and curl refuses before checking the hostname. With --insecure, both checks are skipped: the connection is encrypted, but you no longer know who answered.

steps.label: Both checks pass
steps.text: --cacert makes curl trust the practice issuer, and the certificate is for dispatch.test, so the request continues.

steps.label: An unknown issuer
steps.text: Without --cacert, curl does not trust who issued the certificate and stops immediately.

steps.label: Skipping the checks
steps.text: --insecure skips both checks. The traffic is encrypted, but you cannot know who you are talking to.

title: Gateway API’s links and what breaks them
caption: parentRefs attaches a route to a Gateway; backendRefs sends it to a Service. Status shows which link failed.
description: A sequence in three steps. A GatewayClass named traefik is owned by admins, a Gateway with a listener on 8080 by the platform team, and an HTTPRoute by the app team. The HTTPRoute attaches to the Gateway through parentRefs and sends traffic to the Service dispatch on port 8080 through backendRefs. When everything links, the route's status shows Accepted, ResolvedRefs, and Programmed all True. When parentRefs names a Gateway that does not exist, there is no entry under Parents at all. When backendRefs uses a port the Service does not have, ResolvedRefs is False.

steps.label: Everything links
steps.text: The route is attached to the Gateway and its backend exists, so Accepted, ResolvedRefs, and Programmed are all True.

steps.label: A missing parent
steps.text: parentRefs names a Gateway that does not exist, so no controller reports on the route: Parents is empty.

steps.label: A wrong backend port
steps.text: The route is attached, but backendRefs names a port the Service does not have, so ResolvedRefs is False.

title: From PostgreSQL’s folder to a disk
caption: Every link must be present; a claim the Pod does not use protects nothing.
description: A chain of six links. PostgreSQL writes its data folder. The container's volumeMounts mount the volume named data there. The Pod's volumes entry says data uses the claim, through claimName. The PersistentVolumeClaim is the request in the dispatch namespace. It is Bound to a PersistentVolume, the real storage, which is cluster-wide. That volume is a disk on the node where the bytes live. A StorageClass named standard provisions the PersistentVolume.

title: Why the claim waits
caption: With WaitForFirstConsumer, storage is created only once Kubernetes knows which node needs it.
description: A sequence in four steps. The claim dispatch-data uses a WaitForFirstConsumer class and is Pending while no Pod uses it. A db Pod that uses the claim is scheduled to a node. The provisioner creates a PersistentVolume on that node. The claim becomes Bound and the Pod runs.

steps.label: No Pod yet
steps.text: Nothing uses the claim, so it stays Pending. This is expected, not an error.

steps.label: A Pod is scheduled
steps.text: A Pod that uses the claim is placed on a node, so Kubernetes now knows where the storage must be.

steps.label: A volume is created there
steps.text: The provisioner creates a PersistentVolume on that node.

steps.label: Bound
steps.text: The claim binds to the new volume, and the Pod starts with its storage mounted.

title: Same name, same claim, new Pod
caption: A replacement db-0 is a new Pod that takes over the old one’s name and storage.
description: A sequence in three steps. The StatefulSet db runs the Pod db-0, with UID 4c1e, attached to the claim data-db-0. The headless Service db-headless, with clusterIP None, gives it the DNS name db-0.db-headless.dispatch. When db-0 is deleted, its claim is kept. The replacement is again named db-0 and reattaches data-db-0, but it has a new UID, 9a7f, because it is a new Pod.

steps.label: db-0 and its claim
steps.text: The StatefulSet’s first Pod is always named db-0 and uses its own claim, data-db-0.

steps.label: db-0 is deleted
steps.text: The Pod is gone, but its claim, and the data on it, remain.

steps.label: A new db-0
steps.text: The replacement gets the same name and the same claim, with a new UID because it is a different Pod.

title: Restore into something separate
caption: Prove a backup by restoring it next to the original, then comparing rows.
description: pg_dump reads the source database in db-0, whose claim is data-db-0, and writes dispatch.sql on your computer. psql restores that file into db-restore-0, which has its own claim data-db-restore-0. Separate claims and volumes mean a bad restore cannot harm the source. A warning says --schema-only produces tables but no rows.

title: What each probe does, and when
caption: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts. Only liveness should ignore dependencies.
description: A sequence in four steps showing the startup probe on /startupz, the liveness probe on /healthz, and the readiness probe on /readyz, beside the Pod's place in the Service endpoints and its restart count. While warming up, only the startup probe checks, and the Pod is not yet in the endpoints. Once started, liveness and readiness pass and the Pod is included. When the database is down, readiness fails and the Pod is removed from the endpoints, but liveness still passes, so nothing restarts. If liveness wrongly uses /readyz, the database outage makes liveness fail too, and restarts keep climbing.

steps.label: Warming up
steps.text: Only the startup probe runs. The Pod receives no traffic yet, and the other probes wait.

steps.label: Started
steps.text: The startup probe has passed. Liveness and readiness both pass, so the Pod is added to the Service’s endpoints.

steps.label: The database goes down
steps.text: Readiness fails, so the Pod stops receiving traffic. Liveness only checks the process, so nothing is restarted.

steps.label: The classic mistake
steps.text: With liveness on /readyz, the same outage makes liveness fail too. Kubernetes restarts the container again and again, which cannot fix the database.

title: A rolling update, one Pod at a time
caption: With maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0, two Pods stay ready throughout.
description: A sequence in five steps for two replicas with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0. The old ReplicaSet runs two ready v1 Pods. A new v2 Pod starts, making three Pods in total. When it is ready, one v1 Pod is removed. A second v2 Pod starts. When it is ready, the last v1 Pod is removed, leaving two ready v2 Pods. Throughout, two Pods are ready.

steps.label: Before the update
steps.text: The old ReplicaSet runs two ready Pods of v1.

steps.label: Surge one new Pod
steps.text: maxSurge 1 allows a third Pod, so the first v2 Pod starts while both v1 Pods keep serving.

steps.label: Replace one old Pod
steps.text: Once the new Pod is ready, one v1 Pod is removed. Two Pods are still ready.

steps.label: Surge again
steps.text: The second v2 Pod starts beside the remaining v1 Pod.

steps.label: Finished
steps.text: The last v1 Pod is removed. The new ReplicaSet runs two ready v2 Pods.

title: How update settings limit the damage
caption: A bad image stalls both rollouts, but only one of them takes the service down.
description: Two panels showing the same missing image. With maxUnavailable 2 and maxSurge 0, both v1 Pods are removed and both v2 Pods cannot start, leaving 0 ready Pods: an outage. With maxUnavailable 0 and maxSurge 1, both v1 Pods stay ready while one v2 Pod cannot start, leaving 2 ready Pods still serving. A note says either way the rollout is stuck, but only one setting keeps Dispatch up.

title: A canary beside the stable release
caption: The main Service selects both tracks; the preview Service selects only the canary.
description: The Service dispatch selects app=dispatch and sends traffic to three Pods: two release 1 Pods from the Deployment dispatch with track=stable, and one release 2 Pod from dispatch-canary with track=canary. The Service dispatch-preview selects track=canary and reaches only the canary Pod. A note says about one in three connections to dispatch reaches the canary.

title: Blue-green: switch everything at once
caption: Changing one selector moves all traffic; changing it back undoes the switch.
description: A sequence in two steps. The Service dispatch has the selector version=blue, so all traffic goes to the two blue Pods running release 1, while the two green Pods running release 2 wait. After the selector changes to version=green, all traffic goes to the green Pods at once, and the blue Pods remain available for a quick switch back.

steps.label: Blue is live
steps.text: The Service selects version=blue, so every request reaches release 1. Green runs release 2 but receives no traffic.

steps.label: Switch to green
steps.text: Changing the selector to version=green moves all traffic to release 2 at once. Blue stays ready in case you switch back.

title: Requests reserve; limits cap
caption: Going over a CPU limit slows a container down; going over a memory limit kills it.
description: Two bars. For CPU, a request of 50m is reserved and the limit is 300m; a busy container is held at the limit and slows down, which is called throttling. For memory, a request of 64Mi is reserved and the limit is 192Mi; a container that uses more than the limit is killed with OOMKilled.

title: Quality of service classes
caption: Requests and limits decide which Pods are evicted first when memory runs short.
description: Three classes from left to right: BestEffort, with no requests or limits; Burstable, with some requests or limits, which includes Dispatch's API; and Guaranteed, with requests equal to limits. When a node runs short of memory, BestEffort Pods are evicted first and Guaranteed Pods last.

title: Taints repel, tolerations allow, affinity attracts
caption: Dedicating nodes takes a taint on the nodes plus a toleration and affinity on the Pod.
description: A sequence in three steps with three nodes: the control plane, tainted control-plane:NoSchedule, and two workers, each tainted pool=apps:NoSchedule and labelled pool=apps. A Dispatch Pod with no toleration is refused by every node because of untolerated taints and stays Pending. With a toleration for pool=apps, the workers allow it but nothing sends it there, and the control plane still refuses. With the toleration and affinity for pool=apps, the control plane is excluded because it is not pool=apps, and Pods are placed on the workers.

steps.label: Taints keep it out
steps.text: Every node has a taint the Pod does not tolerate, so it stays Pending.

steps.label: A toleration only allows
steps.text: The workers now allow the Pod, but a toleration never sends a Pod anywhere.

steps.label: Affinity sends it there
steps.text: Affinity requires pool=apps nodes, so the Pod is placed on the workers, while their taint keeps other Pods away.

title: Spreading copies across nodes
caption: maxSkew limits how uneven the copies may be across the chosen topology.
description: Two panels, each with two worker nodes. Without a spread rule, both Pods can land on one node, a skew of 2. With maxSkew 1 by hostname, the Pods are placed one on each node, a skew of 0.

title: How the HPA chooses a replica count
caption: Utilization is measured against the request, then the result is kept between min and max.
description: The Metrics Server measures each Pod, the HPA compares the measurement with its target, and the Deployment is scaled from 2 to 4 replicas, repeating every few seconds. The calculation: the target is 50% of the 50m request, so aim for 25m per Pod; the measured average use is 100m per Pod, 200%; desired is 2 Pods times 200% divided by 50%, which is 8 Pods; capped at maxReplicas, that is 4 Pods, and the HPA reports ScalingLimited.

title: A drain that respects a PodDisruptionBudget
caption: Evictions wait whenever one more would take the application below its minimum.
description: A sequence in five steps with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable 2. At first worker runs Pods A and B and worker2 runs Pod C, so 3 are ready. Draining cordons worker and evicts Pod A; its replacement A′ starts on worker2, leaving 2 ready. Pod B must wait, because evicting it would leave only 1 ready. Once A′ is ready, B is evicted and B′ starts, still 2 ready. Finally all three run on worker2 and 3 are ready.

steps.label: Before the drain
steps.text: Three Pods are ready, one more than the budget’s minimum of two.

steps.label: Evict one Pod
steps.text: The drain cordons worker and evicts Pod A. Its replacement starts on worker2, and two Pods stay ready.

steps.label: The next eviction waits
steps.text: Evicting Pod B now would leave one ready Pod, below the minimum, so the drain waits.

steps.label: Continue
steps.text: With A′ ready, Pod B can be evicted, and its replacement starts on worker2.

steps.label: The drain completes
steps.text: worker is empty and all three Pods run on worker2. The budget was never broken.

title: Why a short preStop helps
caption: The pause lets the Service stop sending traffic before the process begins to exit.
description: A timeline from the moment a Pod is deleted. On the Service lane, the endpoint is being removed for the first moments, and after that no new traffic arrives. On the container lane, the preStop hook sleeps for 5 seconds while still serving, then SIGTERM arrives and the process exits. The grace period ends at 20 seconds.

title: One base, one overlay per environment
caption: Each overlay starts from the shared base and records only what differs.
description: The base folder holds deployment.yaml, service.yaml, configmap.yaml, and kustomization.yaml. The development overlay uses the base and sets namespace dispatch, replicas 2, and environment development, producing the development manifests that are deployed in this lab. The staging overlay uses the same base and sets namespace staging and environment staging, producing manifests that are only rendered here.

title: From values to a release
caption: Helm fills the chart’s templates with the combined values, then records the result as a revision.
description: Values come from three places, from lowest to highest priority: the chart's values.yaml defaults, a file passed with -f such as values-practice.yaml, and --set api.replicas=2; later values win. Helm fills the chart's templates with the combined values and installs the result as the release dispatch, recording revisions 1, 2, 3 and so on. A note says helm template shows the filled-in manifests without installing anything.

title: Revisions, a bad upgrade, and a rollback
caption: A rollback makes a new revision from an old one, but leaves your values file unchanged.
description: A sequence in three steps. Revision 1 runs 2 replicas and serves. Revision 2 sets 0 replicas; Helm reports it as deployed, but 0 Pods are serving. Rolling back to revision 1 creates revision 3, which reuses revision 1's manifests and values and serves again. The file values-practice.yaml still says replicas: 0.

steps.label: A healthy release
steps.text: Revision 1 runs two replicas and serves requests.

steps.label: A bad upgrade
steps.text: Revision 2 asks for zero replicas. Helm reports deployed, because nothing it waited for failed, yet no Pod is serving.

steps.label: Roll back
steps.text: helm rollback creates revision 3 from revision 1. The release serves again, but values-practice.yaml still says zero, so fix it too.

title: An operator restoring drift
caption: The custom resource is the source of truth; the controller keeps the Deployment matching it.
description: A sequence in three steps. The WorkerPool dispatch asks for 2 replicas, the workerpool-controller watches it and manages the Deployment dispatch-workers at 2 replicas, and two worker Pods are ready, so the WorkerPool status shows Ready True. Someone scales the Deployment to 0 by hand, the worker Pods terminate, and status shows Ready False. The controller notices the drift and sets the Deployment back to 2, starting new workers and returning to Ready True.

steps.label: Matching the WorkerPool
steps.text: The controller keeps dispatch-workers at the two replicas the WorkerPool asks for, and reports Ready.

steps.label: Changed by hand
steps.text: Scaling the Deployment directly to zero stops the workers, and the status reports the mismatch.

steps.label: Put back
steps.text: On its next pass the controller sets the Deployment back to two, because the WorkerPool still says two.

title: Three kinds of evidence
caption: Each source answers a different question; one alone can mislead you.
description: Three panels. Events show what Kubernetes noticed, such as Scheduled, Pulled, and Unhealthy when a probe failed. Logs show what the application said, such as GET /jobs 200 lines taking 12, 15, and 640 milliseconds. Metrics show how it behaves over time, as a response-time line rising sharply. A note says a Pod can be Running, with clean-looking logs, and still serve every request slowly, so use all three.

title: Why you take the rate of a counter
caption: A counter drops to zero when its process restarts; rate() measures growth and copes with the reset.
description: Two charts over the same time. The counter dispatch_http_requests_total climbs steadily, drops to zero when the Pod restarts, then climbs again. Below it, rate over two minutes, the requests per second, stays level through the restart.

title: How Prometheus chooses what to scrape
caption: Relabel rules decide which Pods are targets and how their series are labelled.
description: Prometheus asks the Kubernetes API which Pods exist, then applies relabel rules that keep only Pods labelled app=dispatch with a container port named http. Dispatch Pods A and B are kept and scraped directly, each with its own pod label; the db Pod is dropped. Prometheus scrapes every five seconds.

title: From histogram buckets to a slow fraction
caption: Divide the bucket at your threshold by the total count, then subtract from one.
description: A bar chart of 200 requests in cumulative buckets: 120 at or under 0.1 seconds, 170 at or under 0.25 seconds, 190 at or under 0.5 seconds, 198 at or under 1 second, and 200 in all. Each bucket counts every request at or under its limit. Fast enough is 170 divided by 200, which is 85%. Too slow is 1 minus 0.85, which is 15%. Since 15% is above the 10% threshold, the alert condition is true.

title: Pending, firing, resolved
caption: for: 15s holds the alert in pending until the condition has lasted fifteen seconds.
description: A timeline with two rows. The condition, slow fraction above 10%, is false at first, true from when the slowdown starts until speed is restored, then false again. The alert is inactive at first, pending for the first 15 seconds of the slowdown, firing from then until speed is restored, and then resolved.

title: An error budget of ten reads
caption: The objective decides how many bad events you can afford before the SLO is missed.
description: A grid of 200 squares, one for each eligible GET /jobs read: 190 are good and the last 10 are marked as the error budget. With an objective of 95% good, at most 10 reads may be bad. A read is bad if it fails, or if it succeeds but takes over 250 milliseconds.

title: A test gate in the pipeline
caption: A gate only protects you if a failure really stops the steps after it.
description: A sequence in three steps through four pipeline stages: build, test, push, and record. With tests switched off, the test is skipped and anything that builds is pushed and recorded. With a failing test, the test reports FAIL with exit 1, and push and record do not run. With passing tests, the test reports OK with exit 0, the image is pushed, and release.json records the exact digest that passed.

steps.label: Tests switched off
steps.text: The test stage is skipped, so any image that builds is pushed and recorded.

steps.label: A failing test
steps.text: The test exits 1, so the pipeline stops: nothing is pushed or recorded.

steps.label: Tests pass
steps.text: The image is pushed, and release.json records its digest and the source fingerprints.

title: The GitOps loop
caption: To change what runs, change Git; changes made only in the cluster do not last.
description: You commit and push to the Git repository delivery, which holds the desired state. Flux fetches it, builds it, and applies it to the dispatch namespace as the ServiceAccount dispatch-deployer, so the Deployment dispatch matches what Git declares. A change made by hand with kubectl, which Git does not know about, is undone on Flux's next pass.

title: Promote by digest, roll back through Git
caption: Staging receives the exact image development tested, and a bad change is undone by a new commit.
description: A sequence in four steps with the Git history in delivery beside the development and staging environments. Commit a1 sets development to the image sha256:7c9…, which becomes ready. Commit b2 promotes the same digest to staging. Commit c3 sets staging to a missing image; the new staging Pod cannot pull it while the old Pod keeps serving. Commit d4 reverts c3, and staging is ready again on sha256:7c9….

steps.label: Release to development
steps.text: A commit sets development to the tested image digest, and Flux applies it.

steps.label: Promote the same digest
steps.text: A separate commit gives staging the exact same digest, not a rebuild.

steps.label: A bad commit
steps.text: Staging is pointed at an image that does not exist. The new Pod cannot pull it; the old Pod keeps serving because maxUnavailable is 0.

steps.label: Revert in Git
steps.text: git revert adds a commit that undoes the mistake, and Flux returns staging to the good digest.

title: How far a binding reaches
caption: Where a permission applies depends on the binding, not on where the rules were written.
description: Three combinations and their reach across the dispatch namespace, other namespaces, and cluster-wide objects such as nodes and PersistentVolumes. A Role with a RoleBinding grants access only in dispatch. A ClusterRole with a RoleBinding also grants access only in dispatch. A ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding grants access everywhere, including other namespaces and cluster-wide objects.

title: Removing access the reader does not need
caption: Least privilege keeps the useful permission and removes the rest, and you test both.
description: A sequence in two steps showing the Role dispatch-pod-reader beside kubectl auth can-i answers for dispatch-reader. At first the rule allows get, list, and watch on pods and secrets, so listing Pods in dispatch says yes, getting Secrets in dispatch also says yes, which is too much, and listing Pods in kube-system says no. After removing secrets from the rule, the answers are yes, no, and no.

steps.label: Too much access
steps.text: The rule includes secrets, so the Pod reader can also read every Secret in the namespace.

steps.label: Only what it needs
steps.text: With secrets removed, listing Pods still works, and reading Secrets is refused.

title: From open, to closed, to exactly what is needed
caption: Start from default deny, then allow each path the application really uses.
description: A sequence in three steps with a frontend namespace holding trusted and untrusted Pods, DNS in kube-system, and a dispatch namespace holding the API, a worker, PostgreSQL, and Redis. With no policy, every connection is allowed. With default deny, every connection is blocked, including DNS lookups. With allow rules added, the trusted frontend can reach the API, the API can reach PostgreSQL, the worker can reach Redis and DNS, and the untrusted frontend Pod is still blocked.

steps.label: No policy
steps.text: Without any NetworkPolicy, every Pod can connect to every other Pod.

steps.label: Default deny
steps.text: A policy selecting every Pod with no rules blocks everything, including DNS lookups.

steps.label: Allow what is needed
steps.text: Specific allow rules reopen only the paths Dispatch uses. The untrusted Pod stays blocked.

title: One dash changes the meaning
caption: Selectors in one list item must all match; selectors in separate items each allow traffic on their own.
description: Two versions of a from list. In the first, namespaceSelector for the frontend namespace and podSelector for app trusted are in one list item, so both must match: a trusted Pod in frontend is allowed, and any other Pod is not. In the second, a dash before podSelector makes them two list items, so either is enough: any Pod in frontend is allowed, and so is a trusted Pod anywhere in the policy's own namespace.

title: Admission at creation, restrictions while running
caption: Admission decides whether a Pod may exist; its security context limits what it can do.
description: A new Pod from a Deployment goes to Pod Security Admission, which enforces the restricted standard for its namespace and is checked once, when the Pod is created. The Pod is either accepted and created, or rejected and never runs. An accepted Pod's running container keeps its securityContext restrictions for its whole life: runAsUser 12000, no capabilities, no new privileges, the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile, and a read-only root filesystem.

title: An SBOM, a scan, and an unused library
caption: Removing a component you never use removes its findings; the base image’s findings still need review.
description: A sequence in two steps. The image contains Alpine base packages, Python packages, Dispatch's code, and the unused library PyJWT 1.7.1. Its SBOM lists PyJWT 1.7.1, and the Trivy scanner, using a dated vulnerability database, reports CVE-2022-29217 along with other findings from the base image. After rebuilding without PyJWT, the SBOM no longer lists it and CVE-2022-29217 is gone, while the base image findings remain and still need review.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: The SBOM lists PyJWT 1.7.1, and the scan reports CVE-2022-29217 in it, even though Dispatch never imports it.

steps.label: After the rebuild
steps.text: Without the unused library, its entry and its finding disappear. The base image’s own findings remain.

title: Rotating a password in the right order
caption: The server, the Secret, and every consumer must all change; restarting the consumers completes it.
description: A sequence in four steps with the API and worker, the Secret, and PostgreSQL. At first PostgreSQL accepts password A, the Secret holds A, and both consumers use A, so logins work. After PostgreSQL is changed to accept B, the consumers still use A and their logins fail. After the Secret is updated to B, the consumers still use A, because they read it only at start. After the consumers restart, they use B, logins work, and the old password A is rejected.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: PostgreSQL, the Secret, and both consumers all use password A.

steps.label: Change PostgreSQL
steps.text: PostgreSQL now accepts only B, so the consumers still using A can no longer log in.

steps.label: Update the Secret
steps.text: The Secret now holds B, but the running consumers read it only when they started, so they still fail.

steps.label: Restart the consumers
steps.text: After restarting, both use B and log in. The old password A is rejected, which proves the rotation.

title: Restoring onto new storage, then switching
caption: Restore beside the original, verify the data, and only then move traffic.
description: A sequence in three steps. The original database db-0 is stopped with its storage data-db-0 kept, the encrypted backup backup.enc is in one place and its key in separate private lab data, and the Service db has no ready database. Restoring decrypts the backup in memory with the key and loads it into db-recovery, which has its own new claim, and the known record is found. Finally the Service db selects recovery: restored, so traffic goes to db-recovery, while the original storage is kept to switch back if needed.

steps.label: After the loss
steps.text: The original database is stopped but its storage is kept. The backup and its key are stored separately.

steps.label: Restore into new storage
steps.text: The backup is decrypted in memory and loaded into db-recovery, on its own claim. The known record is checked before anything else changes.

steps.label: Switch traffic
steps.text: The Service now selects the restored database. The original storage stays, so you can switch back.

title: The layers beneath Kubernetes
caption: kubectl talks to the API; crictl talks to the node’s runtime through the CRI.
description: kubectl talks to the API server, which holds Kubernetes objects. On one node, the kubelet receives the Pods for that node and asks containerd, through the Container Runtime Interface, to run them; containerd listens on a socket under /run/containerd and runs the containers in kubepods.slice cgroups. crictl connects to containerd through the CRI, and ctr talks to containerd directly. A note says kubectl sees objects, while crictl sees what is really running on one node.

title: This module’s two machines
caption: kubectl works from your lab terminal; limactl shell takes you inside a VM.
description: On your computer, the lab terminal runs kubectl, which reaches the API server on the control-plane VM, and limactl shell, which opens a shell inside a VM. The control-plane VM runs the API server, etcd, and a kubelet. The worker VM runs Dispatch's Pods, the database on a local volume, and a kubelet.

title: What changes when the kubelet stops
caption: The application keeps answering while supervision and reporting quietly stop.
description: A sequence in three steps tracking the kubelet service, Dispatch's containers, the node Lease, and the node status. Normally the kubelet is active, the containers answer, the Lease is renewed every few seconds, and the node is Ready. Just after the kubelet stops, the containers still run and answer, the Lease is no longer renewed, and the node still shows a stale Ready. About a minute later the Lease has expired and the node is NotReady, while the containers keep running with nothing to restart them.

steps.label: Healthy
steps.text: The kubelet runs, renews the node’s Lease, and the node is Ready.

steps.label: Just after it stops
steps.text: Containers keep running and answering, but the Lease stops being renewed. The node still looks Ready.

steps.label: About a minute later
steps.text: The Lease has expired, so the node is marked NotReady. Nothing will restart failed containers or start new Pods here.

title: Where each kubectl error comes from
caption: Each failure stops the request at a different stage.
description: A request passes four stages. Connect asks whether anything is listening; failing it gives connection refused. TLS asks whether the client trusts the server; failing it gives an x509 certificate error. Authenticate asks who this is; failing it gives 401 Unauthorized. Authorize asks whether they may do it; failing it gives 403 Forbidden. A note says the error tells you how far the request got, and so which layer to fix.

title: Static Pods come from files
caption: The kubelet runs whatever manifests are in the folder; the API only shows mirrors of them.
description: The folder /etc/kubernetes/manifests holds kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml, and etcd.yaml. The kubelet reads them and runs them, and they appear in the kube-system namespace as the API server, controller manager, scheduler, and etcd. A note says deleting one with kubectl does nothing lasting, because the file brings it back.

title: What kubeadm init does
caption: Each phase builds on the last; the result is a control plane with no Pod network yet.
description: A sequence in four steps. Preflight checks that the runtime works, swap is off, and the required ports are free. Certificates creates a cluster CA, pki/ca.crt, and a certificate for each component. Static Pods writes manifests that the kubelet starts: the API server, controller manager, scheduler, and etcd. Credentials writes admin.conf and stores the configuration. The node is then NotReady because there is no CNI, which is expected until the next lesson. A note says kubeadm init does not install a Pod network or add other machines.

steps.label: Preflight
steps.text: kubeadm checks the machine is ready: a working runtime, swap off, and free ports.

steps.label: Certificates
steps.text: It creates the cluster’s certificate authority and a certificate for each control-plane component.

steps.label: Static Pods
steps.text: It writes the control-plane manifests, and the kubelet starts the API server, controller manager, scheduler, and etcd.

steps.label: Credentials
steps.text: It writes admin.conf. The node stays NotReady until a Pod network is installed.

title: Two address ranges that must not overlap
caption: Machines get addresses from one range, Pods from another.
description: Both VMs have addresses on the VM network, 192.168.104.0/24. Each VM's Pods get addresses from its own part of the Pod network, 10.244.0.0/24 on the control plane and 10.244.1.0/24 on the worker. The Pod network 10.244.0.0/16 does not overlap the VM network.

title: The checks in kubeadm join
caption: The worker checks the cluster, the cluster checks the worker, then the kubelet gets its own credentials.
description: A sequence in four steps between the worker VM running kubeadm join and the API server on the control-plane VM. First the worker checks it has the right cluster, using the CA certificate hash. Second it proves it may join, using the bootstrap token. Third it receives permanent kubelet credentials. Finally it has joined but stays NotReady until a CNI plugin is installed. A note says skipping the CA hash check removes the protection against an impostor.

steps.label: Is this the right cluster?
steps.text: The worker compares the API server’s CA with the hash it was given, so it cannot join an impostor.

steps.label: May I join?
steps.text: The worker presents the short-lived bootstrap token to prove it is allowed.

steps.label: Permanent credentials
steps.text: The cluster gives the worker’s kubelet credentials of its own, so the token is no longer needed.

steps.label: Joined
steps.text: The worker appears as a node, NotReady until the Pod network is installed.

title: A request between Pods on different machines
caption: Calico wraps Pod traffic in ordinary packets between the VMs.
description: The frontend Pod, for example at 10.244.0.12 on the control-plane VM, sends a request to the API Pod, for example at 10.244.1.7 on the worker VM. calico-node on each VM wraps the Pod-to-Pod packet with VXLAN inside an ordinary packet between the two VMs' own addresses. A note says Ready nodes do not prove this path works; a real cross-node request does.

title: A highly available control plane
caption: Clients use one address; each control-plane node runs its own API server and etcd member.
description: kubectl and the kubelets connect to HAProxy, one stable address, which forwards only to healthy API servers. Behind it are three control-plane nodes, each running an API server and a stacked etcd member.

title: Cordon, evict, replace, schedule
caption: Four separate things happen during a drain; any of them can be where it gets stuck.
