description: A sequence in four steps with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable 1. Before, worker runs one API copy and PostgreSQL with its local volume, and worker2 runs the other API copy and calico-node. Cordoning marks worker2 SchedulingDisabled while its Pods stay. Evicting removes worker2's API copy, which the budget allows, and ignores the calico-node DaemonSet Pod. Finally the Deployment's replacement Pod is scheduled on worker.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: One API copy runs on each worker. PostgreSQL stays with its local volume on worker.

steps.label: Cordon
steps.text: worker2 is marked unschedulable, so nothing new lands there. Its Pods keep running.

steps.label: Evict
steps.text: The budget allows one disruption, so the API copy is evicted. The DaemonSet Pod is ignored.

steps.label: Replace and schedule
steps.text: The Deployment creates a replacement, and the scheduler places it on worker.

title: The order of a kubeadm upgrade
caption: Upgrade the control plane first, then each worker, moving one minor version at a time.
description: The upgrade goes from 1.36.5 to 1.37.1, one minor version. On the control-plane node: upgrade the kubeadm package, run kubeadm upgrade plan, run kubeadm upgrade apply v1.37.1, drain and upgrade the kubelet and kubectl packages, daemon-reload and restart the kubelet, then uncordon. On each worker, one at a time: upgrade the kubeadm package, run kubeadm upgrade node, drain and upgrade the kubelet and kubectl packages, daemon-reload and restart the kubelet, then uncordon. A warning says never to run kubeadm upgrade apply on a worker.

title: A renewed file is not a renewed server
caption: Renewing writes a new certificate; restarting the API server makes it serve it.
description: A sequence in three steps on the control-plane VM. At first apiserver.crt has serial A and kube-apiserver serves serial A. After kubeadm certs renew, the file has serial B, signed by the same cluster CA, but the running API server still serves serial A from memory. After its container is stopped with crictl and the kubelet starts it again, it serves serial B. A note says deleting its mirror Pod with kubectl would not reload anything.

steps.label: Before renewal
steps.text: The certificate file and the running API server both have serial A.

steps.label: Renew the file
steps.text: kubeadm writes a new certificate, serial B, from the same CA. The running server still uses A.

steps.label: Restart the container
steps.text: Stopping the container makes the kubelet start a fresh one, which loads and serves serial B.

title: Node status and Pod traffic travel differently
caption: A firewall rule can block Pod traffic while node health still looks perfect.
description: The kubelet on the worker VM reports Ready to the API server on the control-plane VM over the node network. Separately, traffic between the frontend Pod on the control plane and the API Pod on the worker travels as VXLAN on UDP port 4789. An iptables rule in raw PREROUTING on the control plane drops UDP 4789, so the worker's replies never reach the frontend, even though both nodes stay Ready.

title: Each test adds a layer
caption: Start with the narrowest test and add layers until something fails.
description: Four tests, each adding a layer. Requesting the API Pod IP tests packet delivery between nodes. Requesting the Service name adds DNS and Service routing. GET /healthz adds whether the process answers. GET /readyz or a real job adds its database and queue.

title: Naming and routing are separate jobs
caption: CoreDNS turns a name into a ClusterIP; kube-proxy’s rules turn that IP into a Pod.
description: The frontend Pod asks CoreDNS, which reads Services, what dispatch is, and gets back a ClusterIP. It then connects to that ClusterIP, and node rules programmed by kube-proxy send the connection to a dispatch Pod. If DNS fails but the IP works, look at CoreDNS; if DNS works but the IP fails, look at kube-proxy. A note says to test with a new Service, because routes kube-proxy set up earlier keep working after it stops.

title: A volume that cannot follow its Pod
caption: The hostpath volume lives on one worker, so the database must run there.
description: A sequence in three steps. The CSI node plugin is registered on the worker VM, where the hostpath folder holds PV data-db-0. At first db-0 runs on the worker with its volume attached and mounted. After the StatefulSet is changed to run on the control plane, db-0 there cannot use its volume, because the driver is not there and the data lives on the worker. When it is placed on the worker again, db-0 reuses the original claim and data.

steps.label: Healthy
steps.text: The volume was created, attached, and mounted on the worker, where db-0 runs.

steps.label: Moved away
steps.text: The StatefulSet now places db-0 on the control plane, which has neither the driver nor the data.

steps.label: Placed back
steps.text: With the worker required again and the failed Pod deleted, db-0 returns and mounts the same volume.

title: What an etcd snapshot holds
caption: etcd remembers what Kubernetes was told; it does not hold your application’s data.
description: An etcd snapshot holds Kubernetes objects: Deployments and Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets, the database's StatefulSet, and its PersistentVolumeClaim. Dispatch's jobs are rows in PostgreSQL on the worker's volume, which are not in any etcd snapshot. A note says application data needs its own backups.

title: Snapshot, loss, restore, switch
caption: Restore into a new directory, then point etcd at it; the original object returns with its original UID.
description: A sequence in four steps in /var/lib/etcd on the control-plane VM. etcd's live data is in member/, and snapshot save writes dockyard-recovery.db while the ConfigMap maintenance-sentinel exists with UID 7f3…. The ConfigMap is then deleted. snapshot restore writes a new directory, dockyard-restored, with the revision bumped ahead. Finally the etcd.yaml hostPath points to the restored directory, member/ is no longer used, and maintenance-sentinel is back with its original UID 7f3…. A note says recreating it by hand would give it a new UID.

steps.label: Take a snapshot
steps.text: etcdctl snapshot save writes the whole database to one file, while the ConfigMap still exists.

steps.label: Lose something
steps.text: The original maintenance-sentinel ConfigMap is deleted.

steps.label: Restore into a new directory
steps.text: etcdutl writes a complete new data directory from the snapshot, with the revision moved far ahead.

steps.label: Point etcd at it
steps.text: Changing the manifest’s hostPath makes etcd restart on the restored data, and the original ConfigMap returns with its original UID.

title: Two faults, each blocking the other’s fix
caption: The scheduler needs both its file in the folder and a kubelet watching the folder.
description: A sequence in three steps. At first /etc/kubernetes/manifests holds etcd, kube-apiserver, and kube-controller-manager, because kube-scheduler.yaml was moved away, and the kubelet is stopped, so the scheduler is not running and a brand-new Pod stays Pending with no node. After the file is moved back, the kubelet is still stopped, so nothing changes. After the kubelet starts, it runs the scheduler again and a new Pod gets a node. Pods that already had a node keep running throughout.

steps.label: Both broken
steps.text: The scheduler’s file is missing and the kubelet is stopped, so new Pods stay Pending.

steps.label: Put the file back
steps.text: The file is in place, but with the kubelet stopped nothing reads the folder, so nothing changes yet.

steps.label: Start the kubelet
steps.text: The kubelet reads the folder, starts the scheduler, and new Pods get nodes again.

title: An API server that cannot reach etcd
caption: etcd is healthy; the API server is simply looking in the wrong place.
description: A sequence in two steps on the control-plane VM. etcd listens on 127.0.0.1:2379. With --etcd-servers set to a wrong port, the API server cannot reach etcd and exits and restarts again and again, while kubectl cannot connect. With --etcd-servers set to port 2379, the API server connects and becomes ready, and /readyz reports ok.

steps.label: The wrong address
steps.text: The API server looks for etcd on the wrong port, fails, and restarts endlessly. kubectl can only report that it cannot connect.

steps.label: The right address
steps.text: Pointed at port 2379, where etcd really listens, the API server connects and reports ready.

title: The triage loop
caption: One guess, one test, one change at a time, so you always know what helped.
description: Five stages in a loop: observe the symptom in a user's words, guess one cause that explains it, test with a command that proves it either way, change one thing if the test agrees, and check whether the symptom changed. Repeat until the symptom is gone. A note says if a test disagrees with your guess, change the guess, not the cluster.

title: One fault can hide the next
caption: Follow the request through every step until a new job reaches done.
description: A sequence in three steps along the path Service, API, worker, PostgreSQL. At first the Service has no endpoints because of a selector mismatch, so the healthy API is never reached and the later steps cannot be tested. After fixing the selector, the API stores the job as queued, but the worker Deployment is scaled to zero, so the job waits. After the workers are scaled up, the worker processes the job and PostgreSQL saves the result as done.

steps.label: The route is broken
steps.text: The Service selects no Pods, so requests never reach the healthy API. Nothing after it can be tested yet.

steps.label: The next fault appears
steps.text: Requests reach the API and the job is stored, but no worker runs, so it stays queued.

steps.label: Every step works
steps.text: With workers running, the job is processed and saved as done.

title: Doing the sums before scaling
caption: Multiply each copy’s requests and limits by the replica count, then compare with the budget.
description: Each copy requests 25m CPU and 32 MiB, with limits of 300m CPU and 192 MiB. Bars compare totals for 2, 3, and 4 copies with the team's budget. CPU requests total 50m, 75m, and 100m against a budget of 1 CPU. Memory requests total 64, 96, and 128 MiB against 512 MiB. Memory limits total 384, 576, and 768 MiB against 1 GiB. All fit within the budget.

title: Still answering, but not finished
caption: Compare all four counts; available Pods alone do not mean the release succeeded.
description: A sequence in two steps. With the bad image, the Deployment shows desired 2, up-to-date 1, available 2, and total 3: the previous ReplicaSet's two Pods are ready and serving while the newest ReplicaSet's Pod is stuck in ErrImageNeverPull, so the rollout is stuck. After rolling back, all four counts are 2: the newest ReplicaSet's two Pods are ready and serving, the old Pods are scaled away, and the rollout has finished.

steps.label: Stuck
steps.text: Two old Pods still serve, so health checks pass, but one new Pod cannot start and the counts disagree.

steps.label: Finished
steps.text: After the rollback, desired, up-to-date, available, and total all show 2.

title: What happens when you press Enter
caption: The terminal shows text, the shell reads your command, and the program does the work.
description: Three parts from left to right. The terminal window shows the line docker ps that you typed. The shell reads that line, fills in any variables, and starts the program it names. The docker program does the work and prints its output, which appears back in the terminal window for you to read.

title: Relative and absolute paths
caption: A relative path starts where you are; an absolute path starts at the top, written /.
description: A folder tree in four steps. The top folder, written /, holds home and tmp. Inside home is you, inside that is lab, and lab holds a Dockerfile and a site folder with index.html in it. First, the working directory is lab, and pwd prints /home/you/lab. Second, the relative path site/index.html is followed down from lab. Third, the absolute path /tmp/example is followed down from the top, wherever you are. Fourth, cd .. moves the working directory up to you.

steps.label: Where you are
steps.text: Your working directory is lab. pwd prints its absolute path, /home/you/lab.

steps.label: A relative path
steps.text: site/index.html starts from where you are: into site, then the file.

steps.label: An absolute path
steps.text: /tmp/example starts from the top folder, so it means the same file wherever you are.

steps.label: Moving up
steps.text: cd .. moves you up one level, so the working directory becomes you.

title: Reading a command before you run it
caption: Name the program, its arguments, and its options, and replace every placeholder in full.
description: The command kubectl get pods -n dispatch split into its parts: kubectl is the program, get and pods are arguments, and -n dispatch is an option with its value. Below it, the lesson text docker logs <container name> becomes docker logs web when typed: the whole placeholder, including the angle brackets, is replaced.

title: Where a command’s output goes
caption: Output and error messages travel separately, and the exit status reports how the command finished.
description: A sequence in four steps around a command. First, its standard output and standard error both appear in the terminal. Second, > file sends standard output into a file while error messages still reach the screen. Third, a pipe sends the output of printf into sort, which prints the sorted lines. Fourth, every command finishes with an exit status: 0 means success and lets && run the next command, while any other number means a reported problem, and && skips the next command.

steps.label: Two channels
steps.text: By default, standard output and standard error both appear in your terminal.

steps.label: Redirect to a file
steps.text: With > file, standard output goes into the file, while error messages still appear on screen.

steps.label: A pipe
steps.text: With first | second, the first command’s output becomes the second command’s input.

steps.label: The exit status
steps.text: A finished command leaves an exit status: 0 for success, anything else for a problem. && runs the next command only after a 0.

title: Mappings, lists, and scalars
caption: Indentation decides what belongs to what, and nothing warns you when it changes.
description: The example YAML from this guide, with its parts marked in four steps. First, service holds a mapping of six keys indented beneath it. Second, ports holds a list whose one item starts with a dash. Third, values such as 2, true, and the quoted "1.0" are scalars, and the quotes keep 1.0 as text. Fourth, the same file with labels moved two spaces left: labels now sits beside service instead of inside it, and no error appears.

steps.label: A mapping
steps.text: service holds a mapping: the six keys indented beneath it, from name to ports.

steps.label: A list
steps.text: ports holds a list. Each item starts with a dash; this one is itself a small mapping.

steps.label: Scalars
steps.text: Single values. Unquoted 2 and true become a number and a yes/no value; quotes keep "1.0" as text.

steps.label: Indentation decides
steps.text: Move labels two spaces left and it belongs beside service instead of inside it. The file is still valid, so nothing warns you.

title: Three separate checks
caption: Passing one check says nothing about the next.
description: Three gates in a row. First, is it valid YAML: can the text be read at all? Indenting with a tab fails here. Second, is it a valid object: does it have the fields the tool expects? A misspelled field such as replica fails here. Third, does it work: does the running system behave as intended? A Service whose selector matches no Pods passes the first two checks and fails here.

title: Two sets of labels in one Deployment
caption: A Service selector must match the Pod template’s labels, not the Deployment’s own.
description: On the left, the Deployment file with its own label owner: practice under metadata, and the Pod template label app: example under spec.template.metadata. The first label tags the Deployment; the second tags each Pod it creates. On the right, a Service with the selector app: example finds both Pods. A selector of owner: practice would find nothing, because no Pod carries that label.

title: One request, one response
caption: The request says what you want; the response’s status says how it went.
description: On the left, curl sends a request to Dispatch: the method POST, the path /jobs, the header Content-Type: application/json, and the body {"title":"hello"}. On the right, Dispatch sends back a response: the status 201 Created, a Content-Type header, and a body describing the new job with its id and title.

title: Reading a URL
caption: The address picks a machine, the port picks a service on it, and the path picks what you ask for.
description: The URL http://127.0.0.1:8080/jobs split into four parts: http is the protocol, 127.0.0.1 is the machine’s address, 8080 is the port, and /jobs is the path. Below, the machine at 127.0.0.1 runs two services, Dispatch listening on port 8080 and a database on port 5432. The port 8080 selects Dispatch, and the path /jobs selects the jobs list within it rather than /healthz.

title: How far did the request get?
caption: Each error message points at the stage where the request stopped.
description: A request’s journey from curl to the application in four stages, revealed one at a time. Resolving the name fails with Could not resolve host. Connecting to the port fails with Connection refused when nothing listens there, or Timed out when nothing answers. For https, verifying the certificate fails with a certificate or TLS error. Once the service answers, any status code, even an error status, shows the request arrived.

steps.label: Find the address
steps.text: Could not resolve host: the name never became an address, so nothing was contacted.

steps.label: Connect to the port
steps.text: Connection refused: the machine answered, but nothing listens on that port. Timed out: no answer came back at all.

steps.label: Secure the connection
steps.text: For https, a certificate or TLS error means the connection could not be verified.

steps.label: The service answers
steps.text: Any HTTP status means the request arrived and the service replied. Read the status and body.

title: How a short name is completed
caption: A Pod’s DNS settings try its own namespace first.
description: A sequence in three steps. First, a Pod in the dispatch namespace looks up dispatch; its first search suffix makes dispatch.dispatch.svc.cluster.local, which exists, and DNS returns the Service’s ClusterIP. Second, a Pod in the web namespace looks up dispatch; the suffixes make names such as dispatch.web.svc.cluster.local, none of which exist, so the lookup fails. Third, the same Pod looks up dispatch.dispatch, which becomes dispatch.dispatch.svc.cluster.local and resolves.

steps.label: Same namespace
steps.text: From the dispatch namespace, dispatch becomes dispatch.dispatch.svc.cluster.local, which exists.

steps.label: Another namespace
steps.text: From the web namespace, dispatch becomes dispatch.web.svc.cluster.local and similar names. None exists.

steps.label: Name the namespace
steps.text: dispatch.dispatch becomes dispatch.dispatch.svc.cluster.local from any namespace.

title: From a Service name to a Pod
caption: Resolving the name is only the first of three steps.
description: A sequence in three steps. First, a client Pod asks DNS for dispatch and gets the Service’s ClusterIP. Second, traffic sent to that ClusterIP is forwarded to one of the two ready dispatch Pods, its endpoints, and the application answers. Third, both Pods are not ready, so the Service has no ready endpoints: the name still resolves to the same ClusterIP, but the request has nowhere to go and fails.

steps.label: Resolve the name
steps.text: DNS turns dispatch into the Service’s ClusterIP.

steps.label: Forward to an endpoint
steps.text: Traffic to the ClusterIP goes to one of the Service’s ready Pods, and the application answers.

steps.label: No ready endpoints
steps.text: With no ready Pods, the name still resolves, but the request has nowhere to go and fails.

title: Allowing the database but not DNS
caption: A name lookup is traffic too, so an egress policy must allow it.
description: The api Pod has an egress network policy that allows only TCP port 5432 to the database. Its first step, asking CoreDNS on port 53 what postgres means, is blocked, so it never learns the address and the allowed connection to port 5432 is never made. A note says to also allow port 53 over UDP and TCP to the cluster’s DNS.

title: Reading a file’s mode
caption: Three sets of three: the owner, the group, and everyone else.
description: The mode -rw-r----- from the example jobs.db line, in two steps. The first character, a dash, means an ordinary file. The next nine split into three sets: rw- lets the owner, UID 10001, read and write; r-- lets members of group 10001 read; and --- gives everyone else no access. In the second step each set is added up, with r worth 4, w worth 2, and x worth 1, giving 6, 4, and 0: the numeric mode 640.

steps.label: The letters
steps.text: After the type, the nine letters split into three sets: rw- for the owner, r-- for the group, --- for everyone else.

steps.label: The numbers
steps.text: Add r = 4, w = 2, and x = 1 in each set. 6, 4, and 0 make the mode 640.

title: Containers are isolated processes on one kernel
caption: Namespaces limit what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use.
description: One Linux machine with a single kernel along the bottom. Above it run an ordinary process and two containers. Each container is a process wrapped in namespaces, which give it its own process list starting at PID 1, its own network with its own localhost, and its own files. Each also sits in a cgroup with limits, such as 256 MiB of memory for one and half a CPU for the other. Every one of them uses the same kernel.

title: The file changed; the process did not
caption: A program reads its settings when it starts, so check the running process after a change.
description: A sequence in two steps. First, a configuration file on disk is edited to say port 9090, but the running service read the file when it started and still listens on 8080, so systemctl reports active (running) while requests to 9090 fail. Second, after a restart the service reads the file again and listens on 9090, so the file and the running process agree.

steps.label: Edit the file
steps.text: The file now says 9090, but the service read it at startup and still listens on 8080. systemctl still says active (running).

steps.label: Restart, then check
steps.text: After a restart the service reads the file again. A request to 9090 confirms the running process now agrees with the file.

title: The routine for every task
caption: Set the place first and check the result last; flag a task that runs long.
description: Six steps in a loop. Read the whole task and note its context, namespace, and names. Switch to its context and namespace. Generate a starting YAML file with a client dry run. Edit and apply it. Check the working result. Then move on to the next task. A side path flags a task that is taking much longer than its share of the time, so you can return to it at the end.

title: Facts about the Pod, passed down to its container
caption: Environment variables are fixed when the container starts; the labels file is kept current.
description: On the left, the Pod object in the API server holds spec.nodeName worker2, a memory limit of 192Mi, and metadata with the name dispatch-x2l, the namespace dispatch, and the label app=dispatch. On the right, the api container receives DISPATCH_NODE_NAME=worker2, DISPATCH_MEMORY_LIMIT=201326592, DISPATCH_POD_NAME=dispatch-x2l, and DISPATCH_POD_NAMESPACE=dispatch through fieldRef and resourceFieldRef, and a file /etc/podinfo/labels containing app="dispatch" through a downwardAPI volume. A note says the environment is fixed at start while the file is kept current.

title: A higher-priority Pod takes a slot
caption: Preempted Pods are recreated and wait; nothing is scaled down.
description: A sequence in three steps on a node with four slots. First, three batch Pods with priority 1000 and one API Pod fill the node, and a second API Pod waits outside as Pending. Second, the waiting API Pod has priority 100000, so the scheduler preempts one batch Pod. Third, the node holds two batch Pods and two API Pods, and the batch Deployment's replacement Pod waits as Pending.

steps.label: The node is full
steps.text: Three batch Pods and one API Pod hold all four slots, so the second API Pod is Pending.

steps.label: Priority decides
steps.text: The waiting API Pod has priority 100000, above the batch Pods' 1000, so the scheduler preempts one batch Pod.

steps.label: Who waits now
steps.text: The API Pod takes the freed slot. The batch Deployment recreates its Pod, which waits as Pending until room returns.

title: Where an admission policy acts
caption: A policy describes the rule; its binding decides where it applies and what a failure does.
description: A sequence in two steps. First, a request passes through the API server in order: it is authenticated, authorized by RBAC, checked by admission controllers such as Pod Security Admission and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, and only then stored in etcd. Second, a policy holding the CEL rule and a binding naming the dispatch namespace with the Deny action feed the admission stage: a Deployment without a memory limit is denied in dispatch and allowed in sandbox.

steps.label: The request's path
steps.text: Each change is authenticated, authorized, checked by admission controllers, and only then stored.

steps.label: Policy and binding
steps.text: The policy holds the rule; the binding applies it to dispatch with Deny, so only that namespace refuses limitless Deployments.

title: Two ways in with kubectl debug
caption: An ephemeral container joins a running Pod; a debugging copy is a separate Pod with a different command.
description: A sequence in two steps. First, a running API Pod holds the api container, whose process 1 is python app.py; an ephemeral busybox container is added beside it with --target=api, shares its process namespace, and its ps lists python app.py. The Pod is not restarted. Second, a worker Pod whose container keeps crashing is copied into a new Pod called worker-debug, with the same image, environment, and mounts but running sh instead, so its files can be explored; the copy belongs to no Deployment and stays until it is deleted.

steps.label: Ephemeral container
steps.text: Added to a running Pod with its own tools; --target shares the api container's processes, and nothing restarts.

steps.label: Debugging copy
steps.text: A new Pod copied from the crashing one, running sh instead, so you can look around; delete it when you are done.

title: A build argument against a build secret
caption: A build argument is recorded with the step that used it; a secret mount exists only while its step runs.
description: A sequence in two steps. First, docker build passes RELEASE_TOKEN as a build argument into the RUN step that signs the release; the image ends up with a SIGNATURE layer and a history line, RUN |1 RELEASE_TOKEN=dyk_..., that records the token and travels with the image. Second, docker build passes the token with --secret id=release_token; it is mounted at /run/secrets/release_token for that RUN step only, the step reads the file, and the image holds the SIGNATURE layer and a history line showing only the command.

steps.label: Build argument
steps.text: The token's value is saved in the image history with the RUN step that used it.

steps.label: Secret mount
steps.text: The token is a file for one step; the image keeps the signature and the command, never the token.
